public_rationale: Part of the forecast holds. Some countries did look to Europe in 2025. Vietnam passed an AI law in December 2025 that is broadly similar to the EU AI Act's risk-based approach (e2). The 'much of the world' part does not hold. A 2025 study found the AI Act inspired few copycats: only Peru, plus drafts in Canada and Brazil. The UK, Australia, New Zealand, Switzerland, Singapore and Japan took a lighter path (e1). Late in 2025 the EU itself proposed delaying its high-risk rules (e3). The evidence shows a limited EU pull, not broad and growing reliance on Europe.
limitations: 'Much of the world' and 'increasingly' have no stated threshold or baseline.
Evidence relies on secondary analyses rather than a full global survey.

our_interpretation: Plain reading: during 2025, a growing and substantial share of countries would model their AI regulation on the EU approach, chiefly the EU AI Act.
Evidence counts if it shows countries adopting or drafting EU-style AI rules in 2025, or if it shows major economies choosing other approaches.
criteria.support_condition: During 2025 many countries, including major economies, adopt or advance AI laws modelled on the EU AI Act, and analysts describe EU influence as growing.
criteria.contradiction_condition: During 2025 few countries follow the EU model, most major economies choose lighter non-EU approaches, and analysts describe EU influence as limited or fading.

evidence.excerpt: In my study, I found only Canada and Brazil are drafting similar frameworks, and both of those initiatives remain mired in legislative limbo. The UK, Australia, New Zealand, Switzerland, Singapore, and Japan are taking a pro-innovation, less restrictive track on AI regulation.
evidence.explanation: A 2025 study found few countries copying the EU AI Act, and many major economies taking a lighter path. That cuts against 'much of the world' looking to Europe.
